pr.title: coverage: Prefer to visit nodes whose predecessors have been visited
pr.description:
In coverage instrumentation, we need to traverse the control-flow graph and decide what kind of counter (physical counter or counter-expression) should be used for each node that needs a counter.

The existing traversal order is complex and hard to tweak. This new traversal order tries to be a bit more principled, by always preferring to visit nodes whose predecessors have already been visited, which is a good match for how the counter-creation code ends up dealing with a node's in-edges and out-edges.

For several of the coverage tests, this ends up being a strict improvement in reducing the size of the coverage metadata, and also reducing the number of physical counters needed.

(The new traversal should hopefully also allow some further code simplifications in the future.)

---

This is made possible by the separate simplification pass introduced by #133849. Without that, almost any change to the traversal order ends up increasing the size of the expression table or the number of physical counters.
pr.author: Zalathar

processing.reason: PR #133946 is a coverage-instrumentation optimization, not a semantic miscompilation. It replaces `TraverseCoverageGraphWithLoops` with `ReadyFirstTraversal` so that counter-expression creation can reuse more in-edge counters, changing only coverage metadata layout: expression tables, counter IDs, and `.cov-map` bytes. The PR and frozen analysis explicitly state that the old traversal was not incorrect, merely complex and suboptimal; both traversals visit every BCB exactly once and preserve the meaning of the resulting counters/mappings. Consequently there is no source-level original-vs-incorrect transformation whose observable Rust return values should differ. Encoding the old/new traversal as two functions that expose differing counter IDs, expression counts, or allocation order would merely reproduce the intended metadata-layout improvement, not a historically wrong program transformation, and would violate the requirement not to manufacture an unrelated rewrite just to obtain a difference. No valid source-grounded semantic counterexample pair can be constructed for this PR.

analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historical transformation was the loop-first, context-stack traversal order, not a source-level incorrect rewrite and not a semantic correctness bug: it visited a loop's nodes as a batch, using per-loop worklists and special-casing branching versus non-branching successors. That order was suboptimal for counter formation because it did not consistently visit a node only after its predecessors, so counter-creation could allocate physical counters where predecessor counters could instead have formed an expression. The replacement transformation is ready-first traversal driven by unvisited predecessor counts. A reusable lesson is to compare the two traversal strategies on the same coverage graph/function and measure counter IDs and expression tables, while preserving the invariant that every BCB is visited exactly once.
analysis.inputDomain: Coverage-instrumented Rust functions whose BasicCoverageBlock graph contains branches, joins, loops/backedges, match guards, lazy booleans, closures/async/coroutines, or MCDC decisions. For a transformation-difference experiment, use the same Rust source and same coverage graph, changing only the BCB traversal strategy from the old loop-context worklist to ready-first predecessor-count traversal; compare the resulting `.cov-map` counter/expression output.
analysis.originalLogic: During coverage instrumentation, `CountersBuilder` traverses the coverage graph and for each node that needs coverage assigns either a physical counter or a counter-expression, also creating counters on out-edges. The historical `TraverseCoverageGraphWithLoops` used a stack of traversal contexts: one root context plus one per entered loop, each with a worklist. On visiting a loop header it pushed a new context; successors were assigned to the innermost context whose loop header dominated the successor. Successors with more than one successor were pushed to the back, others to the front. The stated intent was that "The traversal tries to ensure that, when a loop is encountered, all nodes within the loop are visited before visiting any nodes outside the loop." The new `ReadyFirstTraversal` instead maintains `n_unvisited_preds`, a `ReadyState` per node, a ready queue, and a fallback queue. It starts from `START_BCB`, yields ready nodes first, and when a node is visited decrements each successor's unvisited-predecessor count, promoting a successor to ready when the count reaches zero.
pitfalls: Do not treat the old traversal as semantically wrong; the PR describes it as complex and hard to tweak and the new order as a strict metadata/counter improvement for several tests.

Do not assume every function gets fewer expressions. The patch shows some `.cov-map` functions, such as `if_let::if_let_chain`, increasing from `Number of expressions: 4` to `Number of expressions: 8`, while still reducing `Highest counter ID seen: c3` to `c2`.
Do not optimize only raw metadata bytes; verify physical counter IDs and expression references remain semantically valid for every mapping and branch.
When a successor is already `Visited`, skip it without decrementing its predecessor count: "The successor was already visited via one of its other predecessors."
Fallback queue entries can be stale after a node is promoted to ready; ignore `Visited` entries and reject unexpected states rather than processing them twice.

Do not `break` out of successor processing merely because one successor is the node itself. The old code warned: "FIXME: This claims to skip just the self-successor, but it actually skips all other successors as well. Does that matter?"
The ready queue invariant is strict: when popping a ready node, its state must be `InReadyQueue`; when promoting a fallback node, the old fallback entry is intentionally left to be ignored later.
preconditions: The coverage graph construction guarantees that the start node is the only node with no predecessors: "We know from coverage graph construction that the start node is the only node with no predecessors."
Every BasicCoverageBlock must be visited exactly once; the new iterator removes the old explicit `is_complete()` check but `ReadyFirstTraversal` still must enqueue all reachable nodes.
A node enters the ready queue only when all its predecessors have been visited: "nodes in the ready queue have no unvisited predecessors".
The separate expression-simplification pass from #133849 is present; without it, changes to traversal order can increase expression-table size or physical counter count.
analysis.summary: InstrumentCoverage counter assignment should traverse the BasicCoverageBlock graph ready-first: always visit nodes whose predecessors have all been visited before falling back to nodes with unvisited predecessors. Replacing the older loop-context worklist traversal with this order lets counter-creation derive more expressions from in-edge counters, reducing physical counters and often reducing expression-table/metadata size. Some tests reduce expression count, but individual functions may have more expressions while still using fewer physical counters, so correctness and total counter use must be checked separately.
analysis.testStrategy: Use the existing coverage golden tests as regression tests: for the same Rust source, generate `.cov-map` with old versus new traversal and inspect `Number of expressions`, `Highest counter ID seen`, branch operands, and raw bytes. The patch updates many `.cov-map` files including branch/guard, branch/if-let, branch/if, branch/lazy-boolean, branch/match-arms, branch/while, closure_macro, closure_macro_async, condition/conditions, conditions, continue, coroutine, inline, loops_branches, mcdc/condition-limit, mcdc/if, and mcdc/inlined_expressions. Add focused traversal tests on synthetic coverage graphs containing branches, joins, nested loops, self-loops, and a node with predecessors visited in different orders; assert every node is yielded once and that a node is never yielded while it still has an unvisited predecessor. Check coverage semantics independently from size: counter/expression IDs may be renumbered, so compare mapping targets and branch truth/false expressions rather than only byte counts.
analysis.trigger: The counter-building traversal encounters coverage graph nodes with multiple predecessors, loop backedges, branch joins, or successors that become reachable from an already-visited predecessor. Traversal order then determines whether a node's in-edge counter can be expressed as a subtraction/addition of existing counters instead of requiring another physical counter.
